title: When You Change Your Mind, Let Everyone Know Why
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Leaders feel pressure to look consistent, so reversing a position can seem like weakness, and many respond by quietly shifting course or insisting nothing has changed. The author argues for the opposite: announce the change as visibly as possible and explain the new evidence or reasoning behind it. Doing so models for the team that the right answer outranks anyone's ego. The post claims that trust rests on a leader reliably moving toward truth, not on never being wrong. A practical payoff is that team members feel permitted to raise risks early and correct course.
points: Quiet hedging and relabeling a reversal as a tactical update undermines the clarity leaders are trying to protect.
Publicly explaining a change of mind, tied to new evidence, is presented as an act of modeling for the team.
Trust is said to come from direction toward truth, not from a record of never being wrong.
Visible course corrections give others permission to surface concerns early.
The author distinguishes consistency of principle, which matters, from consistency of opinion, which does not.
quotes: Creating clarity, setting direction, and getting people on board are big parts of a leader’s job. Once they’ve taken a position on any issue or decision, reversing it can feel like weakness, indecision, or a loss of authority.
Too often, leaders shift direction or reverse a decision without explicitly acknowledging it. They quietly hedge or move away from their original thinking.

They tie all this to new evidence or better reasoning, and clearly explain why they changed their minds. In doing so, they offer the team a model to follow: the right answer matters more than the insecurity or ego of any leader or team member.
Confidence isn’t predicated on never being wrong. It’s built on leaders reliably moving toward truth and good outcomes.

Leaders who update their conclusions and explain their reasoning show others what’s expected. This gives team members permission to surface risks and concerns early and course-correct any time the situation requires it.
Consistency in principle always counts more than consistency in opinion. Teams trust leaders who chase truth over ego, even when it means being visibly wrong.
